en: Here are three ordinary work emails.
One of them is a fake.
Take a look.
Which one feels a little off to you?
It's the password one.
If you spotted it, nicely done.
If not, that's completely normal.
This kind fools about four in ten people.
Let's look at why.
In a couple of minutes, you'll have four simple checks for any email like this.
And one safe move you can always make.
Start with a gut check.
Were you expecting it?
And does it rush you?
An email you didn't expect, that suddenly needs you right now, is worth a second look.
Now, the sender's address.
The name says I.T. Support.
But look closely.
One letter is different.
It's a look-alike, built to pass at a glance.
Then, what it's asking for.
Passwords.
Codes.
Gift cards.
Your I.T. team already has what they need.
They'll never ask for your password by email.
And the link.
Instead of clicking, rest your mouse on it.
The text says your company.
But the real address goes somewhere else.
You don't need all four.
If even one thing feels off, that's enough.
Stop, and report it.
And the safe step is always the same.
Use the Report button, rather than just deleting.
Deleting clears your inbox.
Reporting lets your security team warn everyone else too.
Now you try.
This one arrived this morning, from the boss.
It says:
Quick favour. Are you at your desk?
I'm heading into a board meeting and can't talk.
I need you to buy four one-hundred-euro gift cards for a client thank-you.
Send me the codes here.
And keep it between us for now.
How many signs can you spot?
Take your time.
That one had all four.
When you're ready, give the inbox exercise a go.
A few more emails to practise on.
